study.title: Jeremiah 46 - Judgment on Egypt and hope for Jacob
study.overview: Jeremiah 46 gathers two messages connected with each other: first, the defeat of Egypt before Babylon; then the promise that the LORD will not utterly destroy his people. The chapter shows God ruling the nations, humiliating the military arrogance of Egypt and at the same time preserving Israel in the midst of the punishment. The image is strong: Egypt, which seemed to rise like an invincible flood, is overcome because the day belongs to the LORD of hosts. In the end, the word of judgment against the peoples becomes consolation for Jacob: God disciplines, but does not abandon.

outline.title: Title and defeat announced in Carquemis
outline.explanation: The chapter begins as the word of the LORD against the nations, with an initial focus in Egypt. Jeremiah calls Egypt to war, but soon makes it clear that the panic and escape of the warriors show that the battle is already decided by God. Military pride is undone even before the fight is over.

outline.title: Egypt rises as a river, but falls under the divine decree
outline.explanation: Egypt is described as a powerful flood that promises to cover the land, surrounded by allies and mercenaries. Yet the LORD declares that that day is his day of vengeance. The irony of the text appears when the healing is offered symbolically, but the wound is incurable.

outline.title: The invasion of Nebuchadnezzar and the humiliation of Egyptian cities
outline.explanation: The second message details the coming of Nebuchadnezzar against Egypt and announces the collapse of its defenders. The cities quoted are summoned to prepare, but everything is useless, because the LORD pushes the warriors and causes Egypt to go into captivity. The image of a beautiful calf shows the appearance of force, but destruction comes from the north.

outline.title: Collapse of Egypt and Jacob's preservation
outline.explanation: The text describes the fall of mercenaries and the invasion as a cut from a forest, to the shame of Egypt's daughter. Then the prophecy extends to include the gods, kings, and Pharaoh himself among those who will be punished. The chapter ends with comfort: Jacob will not be destroyed completely, for the LORD is with him and will discipline him with measure.

study.context: The chapter is linked to the scene of confrontation between Egypt and Babylon, especially the Egyptian defeat in Carquemis, mentioned in the text itself. The notes indicate that this event took place in the fourth year of Jeoaquim, and that the Egyptian defeat weakened its claim to dominate the region. The chapter also presupposes the Babylonian threat to Judah, since the fall of Egypt shows that Jerusalem could not rely on that power as political protection.
study.theology: Theologically, Jeremiah 46 affirms God's sovereignty over international history. The LORD does not only act for Israel, but also judge foreign nations for their rebellion and for their confidence in their own strength. The chapter dismantles the illusion of self-reliance: chariots, horses, mercenaries, fortified cities and even national gods cannot resist the divine decree. At the same time, God's sovereignty is not cold or impersonal; it includes proportional discipline for Jacob and merciful preservation of the covenant people. Thus, judgment and hope go together: God overthrows the pride of the nations and keeps their people standing, even if punished.

scholarViews.insight: The text shows that the battle of Carquemis was decisive for the ascension of Babylon and to prove Judah that Egypt could not protect it; Egyptian defeat was already decreed by the LORD.
The chapter begins with the word of the LORD against the nations, showing God as King and Judge of the peoples, who calls the nations to accountability.
The order to rise Gilead and take balm is ironic: Egypt's political wound is declared incurable after its fall.

questions: In what political or human support do I have trusted as if they could save me, when only the LORD rules history?
How does the image of Egypt, strong on the outside, but defeated by divine decree, confronts my tendency to measure security by appearance?
How will the promise that God will not completely destroy Jacob corrects my vision of discipline and hope?
study.practice: This week, examine an area in which you feel tempted to depend more on force, influence, or strategy than obedience to God. Pray acknowledging that the Lord directs the outcome of the nations and also of their lives. If you are going through discipline, do not interpret this as abandonment: seek repentance, perseverance and confidence that God corrects with measure and preserves your people. Also practice humility in evaluating news, power and threats: no human empire is absolute before the God who speaks in Jeremiah 46.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not bring the full continuation of Matthew Henry's commentary in some verses; therefore, his pointing was limited to content explicitly visible in 46:1. It is also not possible to confirm, only by the notes, additional historical details beyond what the chapter itself and the excerpts provide. The use of names and places follows the translation of the presented biblical text, without adding external information.
